headlines.summary: YouTube is targeting more live sports rights. But it's more likely to buy games in bulk if there's a clear consumer proposition underlying the rights.
headlines.article_text: YouTube sports strategy targets more live rights -- but not necessarily events Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points YouTube is scanning the live sports landscape with interest in buying more rights. One strategy of YouTube's is to air some games on its massive free service and put most games on its subscription Premium service. YouTube is still wrestling with the feasibility of becoming the hub of all local games for the NBA starting in 2027. Subscribe here to get access today . Photo illustration of the YouTube TV logo displayed on a smartphone, with the YouTube logo in the background. Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty Images YouTube is stalking the sports landscape for live rights. YouTube would like as many games as it can get its hands on – while also giving users as "clean" of an experience as possible, according to people familiar with the matter. YouTube has been coy with its sports strategy, acquiring the rights to one NFL game last year for its free, ad-supported platform and buying "NFL Sunday Ticket" rights until the end of the 2029-30 season. Beyond those two moves, YouTube has largely been quiet. Still, YouTube is an interested buyer in live sports for almost all of the major U.S. sports leagues if it can get bespoke rights that present an easy consumer message, such as all local games or all games in a tournament, said the people, who asked not to be named because the company's plans are private. YouTube's strategy is distinct from Netflix's — an interesting contrast between the two largest streaming services in the world by users. While Netflix wants individual games or tournaments that it can turn into mini-events, YouTube is more likely to buy games in bulk if there's a clear consumer proposition underlying the rights. In other words, YouTube isn't interested in a swath of games if there's no obvious connection to them. Sports Business Journal reported earlier this year that YouTube is in advanced talks to be the NBA's new regional sports network solution, buying the rights for 20 to 25 teams for a price tag of potentially more than $1 billion. YouTube is interested in the FIFA Men's World Cup rights, as CNBC first reported in July. YouTube is still wrestling with the feasibility of this idea if it can't get all of the teams, said the people. YouTube ideally wants both in-market and out-of-market games, the people said. It's also unclear if the NBA is comfortable selling complete rights to one platform. A big part of YouTube's sports objective relates to building up its premium service. A few weeks ago, YouTube Premium struck a deal to ingest Peacock content within the service for no extra cost. YouTube Premium, which eliminates YouTube ads and costs $15.99 per month, doesn't necessarily want to strike a bunch of other similar deals and turn the service into an aggregator of other companies' streaming services. But what may interest YouTube executives is buying a chunk of live sports and putting it behind the paywall. In other words, making people pay for YouTube Premium to get access to the games. YouTube could then use "free" YouTube as its front-of-the-paywall marketing tool to get people to pay the monthly subscription fee for YouTube Premium. For example, it could put a small number of games on ad-supported YouTube to effectively advertise for signing up for the full package in Premium. It also can use its millions of sports-related content creator videos to push live games on Premium. YouTube hired Justin Connolly away from Disney last year to be its global head of media and sports. Connolly was one of Disney's highest paid executives, having spent 25 years at the company and rising through the ranks to become the company's president of platform distribution, including ESPN and Disney+. Sunday Ticket's fate NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell told CNBC last month the league could redo its existing packaging of games to better fit the modern media landscape. One way of doing this is to deconstruct "Sunday Ticket," which would give the league many more games to sell in other packages. YouTube executives are already considering this as a possibility, said the people. YouTube currently spends $2 billion per year on "Sunday Ticket" and could use that money and more to buy a new, premium package of games if the league moved in that direction. Wolfe Research analysts wrote a note to clients Friday predicting the NFL "will tier its rights in order to maximize the value of premium tiers while setting lower cost tiers to firms with more limited buying power." Josh Boland | Chicago Tribune | Tribune News Service | Getty Images Rivian Automotive on Friday reconfirmed its 2026 vehicle delivery guidance after reporting a year-over-year increase of 46% during the third quarter, topping Wall Street's expectations. The electric vehicle company reported delivery of 19,248 units from July through September, up from 13,201 a year earlier. Wall Street was expecting 18,000 units, according to average estimates compiled by FactSet. Rivian's 2026 guidance for vehicle deliveries, which it raised earlier this year, is between 65,000 and 70,000 vehicles. To achieve that target, the company would need to increase deliveries from the third to fourth quarters by at least 20.5%, to 23,193 vehicles. headlines.summary: South Korea remains cautious on Alaska LNG amid concerns over its high costs and commercial risks.
headlines.article_text: Trump wants South Korea in on Alaska LNG. Here’s why Seoul is cautious Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Alaska LNG would give South Korea a shorter shipping route than U.S. Gulf Coast supplies, but experts say its massive pipeline and development costs could undermine its price competitiveness. South Korea's concerns include potential cost overruns and the risk of locking buyers into long-term LNG contracts as domestic gas demand slows. Experts say greater certainty around project financing, U.S. government support and opportunities for South Korean companies to participate beyond simply buying LNG could be key to broader involvement. In this article @NG26X Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Mike Dunleavy, governor of Alaska, from left, Howard Lutnick, US commerce secretary, US President Donald Trump, Senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican from Alaska, and Doug Burgum, US secretary of the interior, during an announcement in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC, US, on Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026. Trump unveiled plans for South Korea to invest $200 billion in US energy projects, including eight nuclear power plants, a Texas power generation facility and an Alaska natural gas export venture. Photographer: Yuri Gripas/Abaca/Bloomberg via Getty Images Bloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty Images South Korea is taking a cautious approach to the long-planned Alaska liquefied natural gas project, despite U.S. President Donald Trump touting it as part of Seoul's $200 billion investment package in the U.S. Trump said late Wednesday that the two countries had agreed to work on the $50 billion project, but South Korean President Lee Jae Myung pushed back, saying South Korea's participation would hinge on its financial viability and legal compliance. Alaska LNG situation At the heart of the debate is the scale and cost of getting Alaska's vast natural gas resources to overseas buyers. The Alaska LNG project seeks to transport natural gas through an approximately 800-mile pipeline from Prudhoe Bay in Alaska's North Slope to an LNG facility in Nikiski in the south, according to the Alaska Gasline Development Corporation. The integrated project, which would have capacity to produce 20 million metric tons of LNG annually, is estimated to cost between $44.5 billion and $54.5 billion, according to Go Katayama, principal insight analyst at Kpler. Why is South Korea cautious? Shipping LNG from Nikiski to South Korea would take roughly seven to nine days, compared with around 20 to 30 days from the U.S. Gulf Coast, according to Seung Hoon Yoo, professor at the Department of Future Energy Convergence at Seoul National University of Science and Technology. The shorter route could significantly reduce transportation costs and also avoids geopolitical chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz, Yoo said. But those savings come up against the cost of building a roughly 1,300-kilometer pipeline from Alaska's North Slope to the liquefaction terminal in the south. "The economics of Alaska LNG is expensive given the long pipeline versus other LNG projects," said Kit Ling Wong, head of business intelligence for Asia Pacific at Poten & Partners. "It will not be the cheapest supply for South Korea." Wong said LNG supplies from Australia, the U.S. and Qatar would all be cheaper. While Alaska's shorter shipping distance helps, she said the project's overall capex can build three U.S. Gulf projects. For South Korean buyers, the key question is whether the shorter route can translate into a competitive landed LNG price compared with alternatives such as LNG Canada, the U.S. Gulf Coast and Middle Eastern supply, Kpler's Katayama said. South Korea's caution also reflects the risk of cost overruns and uncertainty over long-term LNG demand. The project's lengthy construction timeline and challenging terrain could push costs higher, while slowing demand could leave buyers locked into take-or-pay contracts lasting 20 years or more, Yoo said. Katayama similarly said an expected decline in South Korea's gas demand from the power sector is making buyers more selective about taking on additional long-term LNG commitments. South Korea also has to balance its strategic and trade relationship with the U.S. against the project's commercial merits, Yoo said. Maintaining its focus on commercial viability could help Seoul retain negotiating leverage to seek additional U.S. guarantees or financial support, he added. What still needs to happen? For South Korean buyers and investors, the ultimate test will be the landed cost of Alaska LNG after accounting for feedgas, pipeline, liquefaction, financing, taxation and shipping costs, Katayama said. Greater certainty around the project's fiscal framework, financing, construction and permitting risks, as well as the extent of U.S. government support, will also be important, he added. South Korean commercial involvement in the project remains preliminary. POSCO International has a non-binding agreement covering potential purchases of 1 million metric tons of LNG annually for 20 years as well as steel supply for the pipeline, according to Katayama. He said that the agreement is separate from any broader South Korean government investment commitment. Additional U.S. government support, including tax incentives and financial assistance, would also be important, along with opportunities for South Korean companies to participate in the project's construction, engineering, equipment supply and LNG shipping, rather than serving solely as LNG buyers, Yoo added. — CNBC's Ying Shan Lee contributed to this report.
